title: JAXtari: High-Throughput and Easy-to-Modify Arcade Learning Environment
claim: The incumbent benchmark is widely used but slow and opaque; our reimplementation is orders of magnitude faster, open and modifiable.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; usage plot, throughput plot, closed-vs-open schematic
description: Three-part figure. Left: line chart of cumulative publications from 2015 to 2025 for RL benchmarks. ALE (red) is highest at about 3,500, above MuJoCo, DM Control, Isaac, D4RL and Procgen. Vertical dashed lines mark milestones such as DQN, AlphaGo and ChatGPT. Center: a log-log plot titled Pong, with throughput in steps per second against number of environments. JAXtari-OC (blue, with a rocket) and JAXtari-Pixel (orange) climb toward 100M. EnvPool and ALE-VectorEnv plateau lower, and Gym-ALE (green, with a turtle) stays flat near 1K. Right: two tinted panels. ALE (beige) shows a console and cartridge feeding a black box labeled compiled and closed source, with an actions and observations loop. JAXtari (green) shows a transparent open-source cube, with rendering, modifying and OC-state icons around it.
caption: JAXtari modernizes ALE as a benchmark for scalable and robust evaluation. ALE is the most-used RL benchmark (left), but its setup is constrained by CPU-bound emulation (center), pixel-only observations, and ROM-level barriers to semantic modification (right). JAXtari preserves ALE’s visual fidelity and dynamics, while reimplementing game logic in JAX, enabling acceleratornative throughput, direct source-level modifications, and native access to object-centric and symbolic state.
abstract: The Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) has been a cornerstone of Deep Reinforcement Learning research, providing a standardized benchmark for evaluating general agents. However, its lack of native support for object-extraction and environment modification restricts research into evaluating whether agents learn robust causal models or rely on brittle visual heuristics. Furthermore, the ALE's dependence on CPU-based emulation creates a significant bottleneck in modern GPU-accelerated training pipelines, limiting both experimental scale and iteration frequency. In this work, we introduce JAXtari, an open-source, high-performance reimplementation of Atari 2600 environments. By leveraging massive GPU parallelization, JAXtari allows PPO agents to finish training on 100M environment steps on a single A100-GPU in under an hour. Beyond speed, it provides object-centric observations and a flexible modification system, allowing researchers to, e.g. develop neuro-symbolic methods or discover novel shortcuts and subsequently train and adapt their agents rapidly, sometimes in only minutes.
